definition.text: A layer roughly parallel to the soil surface whose physical, chemical and biological characteristics differ from the layers above and below.

facts.text: Horizons are the product of soil-forming processes; layers that have not undergone such processes are simply called layers.
They are recognised mainly by colour and texture, described in absolute terms or relative to their neighbours, as coarser, sandier or darker.
Given time, an undifferentiated soil evolves a profile of two or more horizons, which differ greatly in thickness and generally lack sharp boundaries.
No soil profile has all the major horizons; some soils, such as Entisols, have only one horizon or none at all.
Erosion can strip upper horizons and bury others downslope, and tillage, tree growth and major earthworks also disturb or erase them.
Going down a profile goes back in time: pollen, testate amoebae and plant remains record past environmental change, and charcoal allows radiocarbon dating of horizons.
Most classification systems use horizons to define soil types, either as whole horizon sequences, as in the German system, or as selected diagnostic horizons.
Horizons are labelled in a shorthand of letters and numbers that describes colour, texture, structure, consistency, roots, pH, voids, boundaries and nodules.

definition.text: The main layers of a soil profile, marked with capital letters, most commonly O, A, E, B, C and R.

facts.text: Many soils have an organic surface layer (O); the mineral soil usually starts with an A horizon, the layer with most organic matter and soil life.
An E horizon is a leached layer, while a B horizon is a well-developed subsoil where substances moving down from the topsoil accumulate.
A C horizon is loose but poorly developed material below, and R is hard bedrock that cannot be excavated by hand.
Mature profiles typically have three basic master horizons, A, B and C; the solum normally comprises the A and B horizons.
Most systems define more horizons and layers than these five, and the letters may differ: the USDA field book adds L for limnic materials, W for water and M for root-limiting manufactured layers.
Suffixes of lowercase letters and figures further differentiate the master horizons.
Because the systems define their symbols differently they cannot be mixed, and none is more correct than another.

title: WRB horizon designations
article: Soil horizon#Horizons and layers according to the World Reference Base for Soil Resources

definition.text: The horizon and layer symbols set out in Chapter 10 of the World Reference Base for Soil Resources manual, 4th edition (2022).

facts.text: It separates organic layers, with at least 20% organic carbon, from organotechnic layers rich in artefacts and from mineral layers.
Fine earth is the soil fraction of 2 mm or less, and the soil surface is taken below any litter layer, which is over 90% recognisable dead plant tissue.
Its master symbols are H, O, A, E, B, C and R, plus I for permanent layers of at least 75% ice and W for water.
H layers are saturated for over 30 consecutive days in most years or are drained, typically peat; O layers are not.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Australian horizon designations
article: Soil horizon#Horizons according to the Australian Soil and Land Survey Field Handbook (2009)

definition.text: The horizon scheme of the Australian Soil and Land Survey Field Handbook (2009), which adds peaty P and D horizons, drops E, and numbers sub-horizons of A and B.

facts.text: P horizons are organic layers formed under waterlogging, named after peats, with 12 to 18% or more organic carbon depending on clay content.
A horizons split into A1 (dark, most biologically active), A2 (paler) and A3 (transitional to B); B horizons split into B1, B2 and B3.
Leached layers are classed as A or B by their other properties, and D marks material below the solum unlike the solum itself.
As a rule of thumb, layers thinner than about 5 cm are described as pans or segregations within a horizon, and excessive subdivision is to be avoided.

notes: FAO (2006) and USDA (2024) designation sections were not drafted separately; their distinctive layers (L, W, M) are folded into Master horizons.

definition.text: A measure of how acidic or basic (alkaline) a soil is.

facts.text: pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of hydronium ion activity; for soils it is measured in a slurry with water or a salt solution such as 0.01 M CaCl2.
Soil pH normally falls between 3 and 10, with 7 neutral; ultra-acidic soils below pH 3.5 and very strongly alkaline soils above pH 9 are rare.
Because the scale is logarithmic, a solution at pH 3.5 has one million times more hydronium ions than one at pH 9.5.
Soil pH is a master variable: it controls the chemical forms of nutrients and the reactions they undergo, and so their availability to plants.
The optimum for most plants is pH 5.5 to 7.5, though many plants have adapted to thrive outside this range.
Most crops do best at pH 6.5 on mineral soils and pH 5.5 on organic soils; highly acidic soils tend to hold toxic amounts of aluminium and manganese.
High-rainfall soils tend to acidify as hydronium ions displace basic cations; in low-rainfall areas unleached calcium pushes pH to 8.5, and exchangeable sodium can raise it to 10.
Soil pH is generally lower where weathering is more advanced.

conflicts.text: In practice, soil pH ranges from 3.5 to 9.5, as values beyond those extremes are toxic to life forms.
conflicts.note: Soil#Reactivity (pH) gives a practical soil range of 3.5–9.5; the Soil pH lead says soil pH normally falls between 3 and 10.

title: Soil pH classes
article: Soil pH#Classification of soil pH ranges

definition.text: The named soil pH ranges of the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, from ultra acidic to very strongly alkaline.

facts.text: Ultra acidic is below 3.5, extremely acidic 3.5–4.4, very strongly acidic 4.5–5.0, strongly acidic 5.1–5.5, moderately acidic 5.6–6.0 and slightly acidic 6.1–6.5.
The neutral class spans pH 6.6–7.3.
Slightly alkaline is 7.4–7.8, moderately alkaline 7.9–8.4, strongly alkaline 8.5–9.0 and very strongly alkaline above 9.0.

definition.text: The field and laboratory methods for determining a soil's pH, from reading the profile and its plants to electronic meters.

facts.text: Profile features hint at pH: poor mixing of the organic layer suggests strong acidity, a caliche layer alkaline conditions, and columnar structure sodic conditions.
Indicator plants help: calcifuges such as heathers, rhododendrons and gorse mark acid soils, and calcicoles such as ash, dogwoods and clematis lime-rich ones.
Cheap kits mix soil with an indicator solution that changes colour; litmus paper dipped in a soil–water mix turns red if the soil is acidic and blue if basic.
Electronic pH meters insert an electrode into moist soil or a soil–water suspension and give a digital reading.
Spectrophotometric methods, developed in the 2010s, add an indicator dye to a soil extract and avoid the drift and suspension effects of glass electrodes.
The USDA laboratory method mixes 20 g of soil with 20 mL of water (1:1), reads pH after standing 1 h, then adds CaCl2 to read it again in 0.01 M CaCl2 at 1:2.

definition.text: The soil pH ranges to which different plant species are adapted.

facts.text: Calcifuges prefer acid soils and calcicoles lime-rich ones; there are more calcicole than calcifuge species, so plant diversity tends to increase from pH 3.5 toward pH 9.
Some species tolerate only a narrow range, such as Monterey pine at pH 4.5–5.2, while vetiver grass tolerates pH 3.0–8.0.
Tolerance can depend on the soil: soybeans may fail at pH 5.5 where molybdenum is low but grow optimally at that pH where it is sufficient.
Breeders use differences between varieties to develop aluminium- and manganese-tolerant cereals for strongly acidic soils.

definition.text: The natural and human influences that set a soil's pH, starting with the minerals of its parent material and the weathering they have undergone.

facts.text: In warm, humid climates soils acidify as weathering products are leached away; in dry climates weaker weathering and leaching leave soils neutral or alkaline.
Rain, at an average pH of 5.6 from dissolved carbon dioxide, leaches basic cations and raises the share of aluminium and hydrogen ions.
Living things add acidity: respiration and decay release CO2, and plants taking up more cations than anions release H+ ions from their roots.
Ammonium fertilizers, acid rain and oxidation of sulfide minerals, as in mine spoil or drained acid sulfate soils, also acidify soils.
Alkalinity rises with weathering or addition of minerals containing sodium, calcium, magnesium and potassium, and with irrigation water rich in bicarbonate.
Carbonates and bicarbonates build up where too little water flows through to leach salts, as under arid conditions or poor internal drainage.
Calcareous soils range from pH 7.0 to 9.5, depending on whether calcium or sodium dominates the soluble cations.

definition.text: Harm to plants from dissolved aluminium, the most widespread problem of acid soils.

facts.text: Aluminium is present in all soils, but toxic dissolved Al3+ is most soluble at low pH; above pH 5.0 most soils hold little soluble aluminium.
Aluminium inhibits root growth: lateral roots and root tips thicken, fine branching is lost and tips may turn brown.
It then disrupts the uptake and transport of calcium and other nutrients, cell division, cell wall formation and enzyme activity.
Acid soils also stress plants through hydrogen and manganese toxicity and calcium and magnesium deficiency; manganese toxicity symptoms appear below pH 5.6.
Acid rain is the main factor mobilising aluminium from natural sources.
The shift from toxic to non-toxic aluminium near pH 5 also marks the passage from acid-tolerant to acid-intolerant soil communities.

title: Soil pH and nutrient availability
article: Soil pH#Nutrient availability in relation to soil pH

definition.text: The control soil pH exerts over which ions are released or held, and so over the availability of plant nutrients.

facts.text: Trading off toxicity against need, most nutrients are best available at moderate pH, although most minerals are more soluble in acid soils.
In very strongly to ultra-acidic soils (pH < 5.0), aluminium-damaged roots take up less, and deficiencies of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium and magnesium are frequent.
Molybdenum becomes more available as pH rises, while zinc, iron, copper and manganese become less available.
High pH lowers micronutrient mobility, a deficit that water-soluble chelates can correct.
Phosphorus was long thought most available near neutrality (pH 6.5–7.5), but between pH 5.5 and 6.5 raising pH may increase, decrease or not affect its availability.
In calcareous soils above 2% calcium carbonate, supplying phosphorus, iron, manganese, copper or zinc is often more efficient than trying to acidify.

title: Soil pH and water availability
article: Soil pH#Water availability in relation to soil pH

definition.text: The ways extreme soil pH reduces the water available to plants and organisms.

facts.text: Strongly alkaline soils are sodic and dispersive, with slow infiltration, low hydraulic conductivity and poor available water capacity.
They are poorly aerated when wet, and when dry they quickly lose plant-available water and become hard and cloddy.
In strongly acidic soils aluminium toxicity limits root growth so much that moisture stress occurs even when the soil is relatively moist.

title: Soil pH and soil organisms
article: Soil pH#pH effects on soil biota

definition.text: The two-way relation between soil pH and the organisms living in the soil.

facts.text: Soil microbes and animals respond to pH directly and through nutrient status, metal toxicity and humus form, so community composition shifts with pH.
At low pH, aluminium-induced oxidative stress harms soft-bodied fauna without an arthropod exoskeleton, such as protists, nematodes, enchytraeids and earthworms.
Many soil fungi acidify soil by excreting oxalic acid, which locks calcium into insoluble calcium oxalate crystals.
Earthworm mucus, weakly alkaline (7.5 < pH < 8), buffers pH, and burrowing animals that mix organic and mineral matter reduce acidity, as in mull humus.

title: Lowering soil pH
article: Soil pH#Decreasing the pH of alkaline soil

definition.text: Reducing the pH of an alkaline soil by adding acidifying agents or acidic organic materials.

facts.text: Elemental sulfur (90–99% S), applied at 300–500 kg/ha, slowly oxidises in the soil to form sulfuric acid.
Ammonium sulfate, ammonium nitrate and urea lower pH because ammonium oxidises to nitric acid; peat and sphagnum moss are acidifying organic materials.
In high-pH soils with more than 2% calcium carbonate, acidifying is very costly and ineffective.

definition.text: A soil's resistance to a change in pH when acid or basic material is added.

facts.text: Within a soil type it rises with cation exchange capacity: pure sand has almost no buffering ability, while soils rich in mineral or organic colloids buffer strongly.
Buffering works through cation exchange and neutralisation, and carbonates also regulate pH; different buffer systems take over at different pH, from calcium carbonate to iron.
It depends on clay content, clay type and organic matter, so clay- and humus-rich soils need more lime for the same change in pH.
Lime must neutralise the acid cations held on colloids (exchangeable acidity), not just free acidity in solution, or the stored cations restore the original pH.
Once colloids are saturated with hydronium, a soil has no buffering capacity left and further acid drives pH lower; extreme rain and heat can also wash out clay and humus.
The lime needed depends on how finely it is ground (mesh size) and on buffering capacity, and can be calculated from initial pH and exchangeable aluminium.

title: Soil color

definition.text: The colour of a soil, often its most visually apparent property.

facts.text: Colour does not itself change how a soil behaves, but it indicates organic matter content, mineralogy, moisture and leaching.
Soils can be brown, red, yellow, black, gray, white or even blue or green, and colour varies across landscapes, between horizons and within a single clod.
Colour develops through chemical and biological weathering, especially redox reactions, as elements released from primary minerals combine into new coloured compounds.
Ordinary conditions give uniform or gradual colour changes, while reducing environments produce disrupted, mottled patterns with points of concentrated colour.
Soil colour is primarily influenced by mineralogy and is often the first impression one has of a soil.
Because colour, especially value, changes with moisture, it may be described both moist and dry.

contested_note: Sources differ on colour's diagnostic value: one says it has little use in predicting soil characteristics, another that it reveals organic matter, mineralogy, moisture and leaching.
notes: Contrast S:7533a1eb22ab (Physical properties of soil#Colour: little use in predicting soil characteristics) with S:450ae7cecf10 (Soil color lead).

title: Munsell soil color charts

definition.text: The standard way soil surveys record soil colour, using the Munsell color system, which specifies a colour by hue, value and chroma.

facts.text: Albert H. Munsell created the system early in the 20th century and the USDA adopted it for soil research in the 1930s; the soil charts keep only the colours most relevant to soil.
Hue is the dominant spectral colour, in soil generally yellow or red, and each page of the Munsell soil colour book shows one hue.
The full system has five principal hues and five intermediates such as YR, each split into steps; charts conventionally show 40 hues in steps of 2.5, such as 10R to 2.5YR.
Value, lightness or darkness, increases from the bottom of each page to the top, lower numbers being darker.
Chroma, intensity or brightness, increases from left to right, higher numbers being more vivid; a chroma of 0 is neutral gray.
General names such as yellowish brown accompany the notation, matching colour chips, but are not formally part of the Munsell system.
Soil counts as moist when adding water no longer changes its colour, and as dry when air-dried.
A colour is written as hue, then value/chroma, as in a Cecil soil horizon recorded as red (10R 4/8) clay; neutral grays are written N with a value, such as N 5/.

notes: Gap-fill: article moved from Soil color#Description to the Munsell color system page; soil-chart facts still cite Soil color.

definition.text: Reading what a soil's colours reveal about its organic matter, iron chemistry, aeration and salts.

facts.text: Dark brown or black usually means high organic matter, which coats mineral particles and darkens them; accumulated charcoal also turns soil black.
Red indicates iron accumulation or oxidation in oxygen-rich, well-aerated soils; yellow also reflects iron, but in less oxygen-rich settings.
Gray or blue marks saturated, anaerobic soils where iron has been reduced or depleted.
Green can come from iron reduction or from minerals such as glauconite, melanterite and celadonite.
White is common where salts, carbonates or calcite accumulate, often in arid environments; jarosite can colour acidic soils yellow.
Sodium helps humus disperse and reach more minerals, so it influences how deep the dark colour extends.
A B horizon, with less organic matter than the A, takes its colour mainly from iron oxides, usually brownish or reddish.

title: Gleying

definition.text: The development of gray or bluish, low-chroma colours in waterlogged soils as iron is reduced or removed.

facts.text: In anaerobic soils microbes reduce iron from the ferric (Fe3+) to the ferrous (Fe2+) form, and less often manganese from Mn4+ to Mn2+.
Reduced iron is soluble and can be removed during prolonged saturation, exposing the light gray of bare silicate minerals.
When the soil dries and oxygen returns, iron re-oxidises locally into yellow-brown, reddish or orange mottles, often along root channels and burrows.
Gleyed material can begin a few centimetres below the surface and continue almost unchanged for many metres.

notes: Process anchored on the Soil color section; Gleysol and Redoximorphic features cover related ground in other chapters.; No article of its own; described in the Gleysol lead and mentioned on Podsolisation, Plinthosol, Brown earth, Blue goo and 1938 USDA soil taxonomy. Greyzem (S:3f0955fc4633) derives gley from a Russian local word meaning 'mucky soil mass', unlike Gleysol's Ukrainian etymology (S:a3d4323c6f8c).

definition.text: An excavation dug to study or sample the composition and structure of the subsurface, usually during a site investigation, soil survey or geological survey; also called a test pit.

facts.text: Pits are dug before construction to find out the geology and water table of a site.
They are usually between 1 and 4 metres deep and dug by hand or with a mechanical digger.
Regulations require pits deeper than 1.2 metres to be secured against collapse if people are to enter them.

definition.text: A cylindrical section of a material such as sediment, rock or soil, usually obtained by drilling with a hollow tube.

facts.text: The sample is pushed more or less intact into the tube, then removed in the laboratory for inspection and analysis.
Hand coring with a hollow tube or piston corer is cheap and quick but reaches only a few decimetres in clay soils.
Coring tools often fracture the core and lose weaker intervals, complicating interpretation; cuttings-based drilling yields no undisturbed core at all.
Dated cores of ocean floor, soil and ice record changes in climate and terrain and have reshaped the history of the Pleistocene.
